Arnold Toynbee (International Affairs, November 1947) attempts the feat of finding a third position, a third force, a third path between capitalist America and communist Russia without becoming fascist. He wants to make Western Europe an independent third factor without allowing Germany to recover its strength.
Europe must not try to become strong again, because Germany might then become strong again.
Better for Europe to perish than for Germany to rise again.
All of this is stated perfectly clearly while remaining peaceful, Erasmian, and never quite spoken outright.
What an immensely cultivated and twisted mind!
In the service of a twisted disposition!

What he calls Western Europe—and from which Germany is excluded—is a bourgeois society in the same social position as the German bourgeoisie in 1919: an intermediate stage between capitalist prosperity and the impoverishment of the underprivileged peoples of Asia.
Germany belongs completely among the underprivileged. So according to Toynbee, Germany has only one option left:
He is the Spengler of the postwar age after the Second World War, just as Churchill became the Clemenceau of the Second World War.
So Claudel has discovered that Germany is the protection and shield of Western Europe against eastern communism (Le Présent, 19 March 1948).

Ernst Jünger says, on the occasion of Arnold Toynbee being brought into the great American defence council, that philosophers of history are now more important than atomic physicists.
As the man who diagnosed the discriminatory concept of war and the transformation of war between states into civil war, I am not surprised.

One becomes even more conscious of Spengler’s genius when comparing him with Toynbee. But Spengler talks too much about Cretans, Hittites, and periods he never experienced himself, but constructed only through parallels, analogies, and similarities.
His universal world history is an imperialist annexation of the past.
Tocqueville is more modest, purer in contemplating his own fate.
Toynbee is both things at once, an English and superior synthesis, but without genuine strength and concerned above all with preventing Germany from rising again.
Perhaps this type of historian has existed only since Versailles in 1919: philosophers of history belonging to decline.

Here a third kind of participant writes history. And Toynbee’s construction of a “third” between West and East—a weak third force whose only purpose is delay—corresponds exactly to this position: the third party sitting between the two sides, the weaker third, the defeated victor.
And for us—and for me personally—very dangerous.

Europe is a balance between land and sea, between oceanic and continental existence, with ports opening both onto the ocean and onto inland seas.
The transition from sailing ships to machines destroyed that balance.
The airplane belongs to the sea in its function as a vehicle, but its advantages ultimately go to the space of the land.

The law governing the seizure of ships and cargo on the high seas arose under the conditions of sailing navigation. It cannot simply continue unchanged in the age of airplanes and radar. That would be like taking rules written for the use of pistols and applying them to atomic bombs.
Russia is land. But the United States is not sea.
The ship called England is not being towed behind a salvage tug. It now sits inside the force field of a remote-control system.

With discriminatory—or “just”—war, meaning the transformation of war between states into civil war and the declaration of the enemy as a criminal, the importance of philosophers of history and augurs necessarily rises.
Undermining an opponent through civil war, and shaking his confidence in his own historical meaning, becomes correspondingly a stronger weapon than the atomic bomb.

I recently read Toynbee’s diagnosis from November 1947, in a lecture published in International Affairs. He asks about a third force between West and East and rejects the idea that Europe should become strong again, because Germany would then become strong again too.

For him this “German crux” is “an insurmountable obstacle to the construction of a European Third Power.” So he would rather let Europe sink and search for a third force without any force.
